- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥0.7) and forecast is rising sharply, reduce peak overshoots by 5–10% to avoid overreacting to short-term sentiment.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.2) and forecast is trending upward, lower the forecast by 2–5% to account for bearish sentiment suppressing price.
- Avoid overreacting to recent spikes: if last 3–5 days show strong upward momentum, cap forecast peak at 1–2% below recent high to prevent lagged overcorrection.
- When sentiment is volatile (alternating 0.3–0.7), apply mean reversion bias: forecast should trend toward 3–5 day moving average, not follow sentiment extremes.
- For 30-day horizon, if sentiment is consistently low (≤0.3) over last 7 days, reduce forecast mean by 3–6% to reflect subdued market participation.
- If forecast is consistently above true outcome by >5% over 3–5 days, adjust downward by 1–2% per day to correct for overconfidence in momentum.
- When sentiment is high but price is flat or declining, reduce forecast slope to avoid “sentiment-driven” false rallies.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if sentiment is weak or mixed, apply a 2–4% downward bias to account for delayed market reaction.
